title: Lisbon: From Rossio to the Castle
intro: Welcome to Lisbon! I'm your guide for the next hour or so. We'll walk from Rossio Square down to the river, then climb up through the old Alfama neighbourhood to the castle on the hill. Keep your phone screen on and your headphones in. When you reach each stop, I'll start talking on my own. If you ever want to hear a stop again, just tap it on the map. Comfortable shoes? Good. Lisbon is a city of seven hills, and we're going to climb one of them. Let's go.

stops.name: Rossio Square
stops.text: You're standing in Rossio, Lisbon's living room for more than eight hundred years. Its official name is Praça Dom Pedro the Fourth, after the king on top of that tall column, but nobody calls it that. Look down at your feet. Those black and white waves are Portuguese pavement, calçada, made by hand, stone by stone. The wave pattern is a nod to the sea that made this country rich. The square hasn't always been a happy place. The grand theatre at the north end was built where the palace of the Inquisition once stood, and public trials and executions were held right here. Today it's coffee, pigeons and people watching. Try a ginjinha, a small cherry liqueur, from one of the tiny bars just off the square. Now head south, toward the river.

stops.name: Santa Justa Lift
stops.text: Look up at the iron tower on your right. That's the Santa Justa Lift, opened in 1902. People often say Gustave Eiffel built it, because it looks like his work, but it was designed by Raoul Mesnier du Ponsard, an engineer born in Porto. It first ran on steam, then switched to electricity a few years later. It's about forty five metres tall and connects the low downtown with the Chiado and Carmo neighbourhood up the hill. Lisbon's hills are so steep that lifts, funiculars and trams aren't for tourists. They're how locals get home. The queue can be long, so here's a tip: you can reach the top platform for free by walking up through Carmo instead. For now, keep going toward the river.

stops.name: Rua Augusta and the Baixa grid
stops.text: Notice how straight these streets are. That's unusual for an old European city, and there's a sad reason for it. On the morning of the first of November, 1755, All Saints' Day, a huge earthquake hit Lisbon. Then came fires, and then a tsunami from the river. Much of downtown was destroyed and tens of thousands of people died. The king's chief minister, the Marquis of Pombal, rebuilt this area as a tidy grid. Inside many of these buildings is a hidden wooden cage frame, designed to flex in an earthquake, one of the first quake-resistant building systems in Europe. The street names still tell you who worked where: Rua do Ouro for goldsmiths, Rua da Prata for silversmiths. Walk on to the big arch ahead.

stops.name: Rua Augusta Arch
stops.text: This is the Rua Augusta Arch, the grand gateway between the city and the river. It was planned right after the earthquake, but it was only finished in 1873, more than a hundred years later. On top, a figure of Glory crowns Genius and Valour. Below them stand Portuguese heroes, including the explorer Vasco da Gama, who reached India by sea, and the Marquis of Pombal himself. The Latin words say, roughly, to the virtues of our ancestors. For a few euros you can take a lift and some stairs to the top, and the view straight down Rua Augusta is worth it. Now walk through the arch and into the huge square on the other side.

stops.name: Praça do Comércio
stops.text: Welcome to Commerce Square. Locals still call it Terreiro do Paço, the Palace Yard, because the royal Ribeira Palace stood here for over two hundred years, until the 1755 earthquake swept it away. The king on horseback in the middle is José the First, who ruled during the disaster. Ships from Brazil, Africa and Asia once unloaded right at this waterfront, which is why the square faces the river like a front door. This square also saw a dark day in 1908, when King Carlos and his eldest son were shot here in their carriage. Two years later, Portugal became a republic. Walk down to the river steps, the Cais das Colunas, to see the Tagus. Then we'll turn left and start climbing toward the cathedral.

stops.name: Lisbon Cathedral
stops.text: This fortress-like church is the Sé, Lisbon's cathedral. Its thick walls and towers look more like a castle than a church, and that's no accident. It was started in 1147, right after Portugal's first king, Afonso Henriques, took Lisbon from the Moors with the help of crusaders passing by on their way to the Holy Land. It has survived several earthquakes, including the one in 1755, though not without damage. Saint Anthony, Lisbon's favourite saint, was born just around the corner and baptised here. Every June the whole city throws him a party with grilled sardines. Watch out for the yellow number 28 tram squeezing past. Now follow the tram tracks uphill, to a viewpoint.

stops.name: Santa Luzia Viewpoint
stops.text: Catch your breath. This is the Miradouro de Santa Luzia, one of the prettiest views in the city. Below you are the red roofs of Alfama, the oldest neighbourhood in Lisbon, and beyond them the wide river Tagus. Alfama survived the 1755 earthquake better than downtown because it sits on solid rock, so its streets are still a tangle of medieval alleys. Look at the blue and white tile panels on the church wall. Tiles like these are called azulejos. One panel shows Commerce Square as it looked before the earthquake, palace and all. Another shows Christian knights attacking the castle in 1147. Evenings around here, you may hear fado, Lisbon's sad and beautiful folk song, drifting out of small restaurants. Just a few steps further is our next stop.

stops.name: Portas do Sol
stops.text: Portas do Sol means Gates of the Sun. One of the gates of the old Moorish city walls stood here. Find the statue of Saint Vincent, Lisbon's patron saint, holding a little boat with two ravens. The legend says that when his body was carried to Lisbon by ship, two ravens guarded it the whole way. That boat and those ravens are still on the city's coat of arms today, and you'll spot them on lamp posts and rubbish bins around town. Across the rooftops you'll see a big white dome. That's the National Pantheon. It took so long to finish, almost three hundred years, that the Portuguese still say a never-ending job is like the works of Santa Engrácia. Last climb now: follow the signs up to the castle.

stops.name: São Jorge Castle
stops.text: You made it to the top. People have lived on this hill for well over two thousand years, because it's the best lookout over the river. The walls you see were built mostly by the Moors, who ruled Lisbon for about four hundred years. In 1147 Afonso Henriques captured it. Legend says a knight named Martim Moniz threw his own body into a closing gate, keeping it open just long enough for the army to get in. He didn't survive, but a square down the hill still carries his name. For centuries this was the royal palace, until the kings moved down to the river. Today it's peaceful, with peacocks wandering between the old trees. You'll need a ticket to go inside, and the sunset from the walls is the best in Lisbon. Thank you for walking with me. Obrigado, and enjoy the city.
